definition.text: Richard B. Norgaard (born 1943) is an American professor emeritus of ecological economics at the University of California, Berkeley, considered one of the field's founders.

facts.text: His research treats development as a process of coevolution between social and environmental systems.
A 1975 paper showed farmers who hired independent pest-control experts earned more and used half as much pesticide as those advised by agribusiness.
He was president of the International Society for Ecological Economics from 1998 to 2001.
In Development Betrayed he argues traditional economics has hijacked the language of development.

definition.text: Robert Ayres (1932–2023) was an American-born physicist and economist who applied the laws of thermodynamics to economics and originated the idea of industrial metabolism.

facts.text: He pioneered the field sometimes called industrial metabolism or industrial ecology, the study of material flows and transformations.
He argued that the first law of thermodynamics makes 'consumption' misleading, because transforming materials unavoidably creates large amounts of waste, some of it toxic.
He criticised growth models whose production functions leave out energy, as if output came from labour and capital alone.
With Benjamin Warr he found growth accounting improves when the efficiency of energy conversion is included.
He is named among the figures of ecological economics.

definition.text: Serge Latouche (born 1940) is a French emeritus professor of economics and one of the best-known advocates of degrowth.

facts.text: He denounces economism, consumer society and the notion of sustainable development, and criticises economic efficiency and economic rationalism.
In Farewell to Growth he credited Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as the main theoretical source of degrowth.
The same manifesto proposes 'ecomunicipalism' to start a virtuous cycle of quiet contraction of economic activity.
